kids.content: RENAISSANCE ARCHITECTURE in GERMANY AND CENTRAL EUROPE 16th-19th Century

By reason of their central position in Europe the teutonic peoples absorbed Renaissance art from Italy to the South and from France to the west, but the distan·ce from the centre of the movement deferred its arrival until some 125 years after its emergence in Italy. The states were distinguished by different geographical conditions, and these differences were reflected in the architecture.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile871.png

kids.content: Timber, brick and stone continued to impart their character to architecture, according to local usage. Moulded and ornamental brickwork was used in great variety in th·e northern alluvial plains. While stone and timber were handled in the vernacular manner of the locality.

The revived classic forms were modified from those of Italy to sait a more northern temperature. Thus windows continued ·to be large, roofs to be steep to throw off snow, and chimneys, necessary for heating, to be prominent features.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile872.png

kids.content: The succession of Charles V to the possessions of the houses of casti.le, Aragon and Burgundy, marks the climax of the German Renaissance. VaFious invasions by the Turks between the years 1529and 1562further complicated matters in Germany, increased the difficulties of the House of Hapsburg, and were iminical tcrarchitectural activities. The wars of Charles V and the catholics against the protestant princes 11547-55) were brought to an end by the Peace Qf Augsburg, which allowed each state to set up what religion it pleased, and to exile individuals who were of different religion from that of prtwailing government.

The growing maladjustment and the political incapacity of both sides culminated in the famous 'Thirty year$· ·was (1618-48} between catholic·and Protestant Princes. These wars not only arrested the development of architecture during the period of their actual prosecution, but also retarded building activities for sometime after the con.clusion of peace.

Renaissance Germany was composed of divers margravates, palatinates, electorates, duchies, ecclesiastical states and imperial cities, subject to different reigning houses of Hapsburg, Hohenzollern, Wittelsbach and Wettin. There obtained a great diversity in artistic development. The Holy Roman Empire still failed to function effectively, even though in 1556 it was separa·ted from Spain and assigned to Ferdinand. Feudalism began to disappear; gunpower changed military methods and bands of mercenaries replaced feudal troops. The principal Renaissance factor was the influence.of the universitities, notably of Heidelberg, the chief seat of the Humanist movement. This was further strengthened by the invention of printing, while in the 18th century, the literary works of winckelmann, Goethe and others
. aroused interest in the architecture of ancient
Martin Luther (1483-1546) to..yers above all other Germans of his time as the dominating
fiaure of the reformation in Germany, and the day in 1517 on which hepublished in Wit-

tenberg his famous thesis against indulgences inaugurated a revolution in the religious life of Germany. He subsequently burnt bull of excommunication issued against him by the Pope, winning support from the rulers of Saxony, Hesse anc;t numerous German rulers. A decree of the Diet of Speyer (1529) forbidding ecclesiastical changes, called forth the protest from Luther and his adherents which originated the name of Protestant. The stress and turmoil in religious thought of this period of upheaval allowed little opportunity for the erection of new churches, but it resulted in the -transformation of those of previous periods to meet the needs of the reformed religion, in the ritual of which preaching became a powerful factor, and necessitated that increased space for seated congregations which brought about the in· traduction of galleries. The strife between protestant and catholics was followed by the counter-reformation! reinforced by the arrival of the Jesuits and the council of trent (1563).

kids.content: The Renaissance style appeared in Germany about 1,550. Approximately, the successive periods were:

list items.content: a. -Early Renaissance (1550-1600) chiefly consisting of the introduction of Renaissance elements into Gothic buildings or of additions to them.

b. Proto-Baroque (1600-60) in which Italian themselves carried the Renaissance from north lta_ly to Switzerland, Austria and Germany, while native architects began successfully to emulate them and produce national versions of the style.

c. Baroque (1600-1710), in which architects principally of native origin but who often had received part of their training in Rome or elsewhere in Italy, brought German architecture to a splendled culimination;
d. Rococo (1710-60), an extension of the Baro(lue period wherein architecture and decoration show great refinement and technical mastery but less vigour and force.
e. Antiquarian (1760-1830), in which there is a progressive return to ancient classical models, the Greek revival being a manifestation and somewhat beyond the period 1790-1830.

kids.content: Broadly speaking the greatest works of the German Renaissance date from the hun.dred years 1660-1760, the Baroqu_e suited the people, peasant and patrician alike, in its intensely visual appeal; the rich profusion of ornamentation in chu.rch interiors was not wilful display but told the Bible story much as hieroglyphs, moral reliefs or stained glass had carried the religious message in other times and places.

Church and palace interiors may sometimes appear over-ornate, even gaudy, but the opulent magnificence that frequ_ently resulted was a direct response to social, religious and political circumstances, and just as spontaneous as the gaiety universally manifested in peasant art. Ornamentation was deliberate and purposeful, and had a greater part in ecclesiastical, particularly Jesuit, buildings than in secular architecture, which was relatively plain, except in the case of the mansionsand country residences of the nobility, where it was appropriate to express gr-acious living.

1. Heidelberg Csstle (1531-1612) -welt exemplifies progressive developments of the Early Renaissance in the various additions to the Mediaeval castle. The later of them suffer from over-ornamentation. There is a great watch tower and an irregular court around which are grouped the Renaissance buildings.

The Saalbau, the northeast corner shows Gothic features mingled with those of the incoming Renaissance: This is relatively plain. The Heinrichsbau, has superimposed tonic and Corinthian pilasters and half columns, two light windows showing venetian affinities, and symbolic statues in 'niches'.

kids.content: 1. The Theatine Church, Munich (1663-90) by A. Barelli and H. Zulalli, is an instance of the developed style. It is based upon the church of St. Andrea della Valle at Rome. The west facade has two tiers of orders, the being linked to the nave by swept buttresses, while twin western towers rise through th· .ree storeys of orders to oddly coarse scroll-buttressed "helms'. A lanterned dome over the crossing completes the impressive scheme.
•Helm - Bulbous termination to the top of a tower, found principally in central and eastern Europe.

kids.content: 2. The Monastery, Melk one of the most striking monuments of the Baroque period. The abbey buildings mount in stages atthe crest of a deep-sided rocky ridge, riding high above the wood-fringed river Danube; western towers with helms of intriguing profile serve as foil to the softly-moulded contours of the crowning dome. The grand effect arise principally from the disposition of the building-masses on the rising site.

kids.content: West of the Urals, Russia covers 2,100,000 square miles (5,500,000 km2). In a land of such enormous distances, and with a highly centralized government, Renaissance architecture was established in the capital city as an importation from abroad. Provincial buildings then followed suit.

Building stone has never been a feature of Russian architecture. The forest of the north provided ample supplied· of wood, which was in almost universal use for smaller domestic buildings and influenced the designed churches. But throughout the vast plain which is Russia proper, the main material of Renaissance buildings is brick.
The severe northern climate called for high-pitched roofs and the onion domes on buildings which are indigenous to the country.

The history of Russian architecture is not one of continuous development, but of separate phases, each resulting from political events and associated with the arrival of foreign architects on Russian soil. Early mediaeval church architecture derives from Byzantine culture, which was brought to Kiev with orthodox christianity in the 10th century.

In the third decade of the 13th century Russia was overrun by the tartars and cut off from the rest .of Europe, with an almost complete cersation of artistic activity for a century and a half. When the new Russia emerged, centred on Moscow, Ivan Ill (1462-1505) the ruler to take the title of Tsar, Sent for Italian architects to reconstruct the Kremlin.

A third dramatic change of direction occured with the founding of St. Petersburg by Peter the great in 1703, and the construction of his new capital as a window on the west. This 3rd period merits more recognition that it usually receives, as a vigor achievement of Baroque and Classicism on a scale unequalled in any other city.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile893.png

kids.content: The brick walls and towers of the Moscow Kremlin, and the Cathedral of the Dormition {the coronation church of the Tsars) were built by Italian architects in the last quarter of the 15th centu,Y, but deliberately related to medieval Russian prototypes. In the 16th century, side by side with the many domes of monastic foundations, a new type of Votive church appeared in the form of an Octagonal tower crowned with a tent-shaped roof. Bar<)que ornament applied in contrasting colour to these varied forms produced a picturesque blend of Russian and western architecture, the 'Moscow' or 'Naryshkin' Baroque.

St. Petersburg, the t1rst great City ot mooern ttmes to oe ouut to a pre-determined plan, reflects the taste of Peter the Great and his successors, and their choice or architects. Although largely by foreigners, the buildings show a vastness of scale, an exuberance and use of colour which are essentially Russian. Secular architecture is4)redominant, and the granite quays of the neva, the intersecting canals and the immense squares are lined with great palaces and public buildings of brick, plastered and painted yellow, blue or green, to offset the white of classical orders and decoration.

The design of all buildings was controllea and none were allowed higher than the winter palace, except for the occasional gilt needle-spire or church dome punctuating the skyline. Such interiors as have survived are respondent with glittering chandeliers and marble col-umns,

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile894.png

The walls are of pink bricks. with coJonnettes, window surrounds and parapets of white stone, a bulbous gift cupola at the summit, and four others at mid-height.

forms to the needs of the Orthodox church.

The Ekaterininsky {Catherine) palaca (1749-56) is no less than 298m in length. Above a basement storey, the giant Corinthian order of the principal and attic storeys carries a balustrade and broken pediments. The facade is broken down into sections. with groups of columns supported by caryatids, and varied treatment of windows. The huge scale the white columns and blue walls, the gult domes of the chapel, are all unmistakeably Russian.

kids.content: RENAISSANCE ARCHITECTURE in BELGIUM AND THE NETHERLANDS

The Netherlands is a term formerly embraced the whole of the 'Nederland' tHollandl and Belgium. The movement of power and commerce from the mediterranean to the Atlantic and Northern sea of Europe placed the low countries in a favourabJe central position 'to share in the new sea power, trade, world exploration and colonial expansion; at the sametime they were directly in the path of conflicts between the major powers.

The period opens with Antwerp.! After the establishment of the Dutch republic ( 1588! the ports of Zealand, the Zuider Zee, and especially of Amsterdam and Rotterdam, rose to supremacy. The Dutch develpped as an energetic and seafaring nation. In the 17th century, the Dutch began their great engineering feats of draining and reclaiming land, of building polders. dykes and canals. of which they have long been famous.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile899.png

kids.content: THE NETHERLANDS IN THE SEVENTEETH CENTURY

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile900.png

kids.content: Stone, brick and marbles continued to be the chief building materials of Belgium, together with the timber of the Ardennes. In Holland, bricks made _from her clay soil created her · relatively sober national architecture.

There are two main climatic zones in the low countries, the one relating to the_l highlands of eastern Belgium and Dutch Limburg, and the other to the low-lying parts of the Flemish and Dutch coastal areas. The architecture of Holland is greatly influenced by its sea-girt, river intersected and low-lying, ten character, where the frequently driving rains, the winds and clear light produced a simplicity of facade and large windows, with c9mpositions conceived in terms of planes rather than sculptural form. Such circumstances apply less strongly to lowland Belgium.

The 17th century in Belgium was not a peaceful one, and, with. the decay of Antwerp's trade her prosperity suffered greatly. In the 18th century, Spanish authority was followed by a period of French rule (1700-6) and under the treaty of Utrecht (1713) the country passed to Australia. Though equally plagued by wars in the 17th century, the Dutch Republic, dominated by the rich and highly urbanized province of Holland, became a great naval power and maritime trading nation with overseas colonies.

The Kingdom of the Netherlands, including Belgium, Holla'1d and Luxembourg created in 1815 with Wiltiam I of orange as its head. The rule of the Dutch king was unwise, and situation so disadvantageous to the Belgians·that they revolted and became a separate Kingdom in 1830.

As the properity of the South waned, the fortunes of the North greew and reached a climax at the 'Golden' 17th century, with the Dutch Republic as a great European power. The power of wealth through trade was largely in the hands of the burgher class, principally of the pr9vinces of Holland and Zealand·, within the semi-monarchial Republic, the princess of Orange has a court which increasingly looked to France for a lead i(l taste and fashions. The burghers followed the court in its patronage of arts, and their houses were richly decorated and furnished, giving a lively. Market for the many artists of this great period of Dutch art.

The beliefs of Luther and Calvin were received early in the low countries, but since Charles V and Philipp II rulers during the greater part of the 16th century, regarded the catholic church and the state as indivisible, Protestants were presecuted. However, the revolt and war against the Spaniards became more than religious: Indeed the Protestant Prince of Orange led armies which included a minority of catholics.

The Spanish Netherlands (lat'er Belgium} remained almost wholly catholic and followed the lead of Rome in church building, wherein as elseWhere, the Baroque style was favoured by the Jesuits. The Dutch, after first adapting and even copying the old churches and setting and enormous pulpit halfway along th.e side of the nave, arranging 'pews to face it, ex-
with a variety o.f central plans which were developed to suit the Refc;mned religion and taste.

kids.content: The Early Renaissance became notable in 1515. Its strong individually is mainly due national conditions and characteristics. It is rich externally and internally, is rarely grand in scale and, due to the northern climate windows in domestic work are even larger than the French and may occupy almost as much space as wall. Architectural details prdgressivefy assume a more authentic Italian character, but methods of composition are in a variety ot ways unique. The .Early Renaissance of Belgium continued until the end of the 16th century.

For the 17th century, it is essential to speak separately of Belgium and Holland. Belgium progressed with its individualistic interpretation of the Italian Pro-Baroque flourishing at that time, to a style which may be described as Baroque. In the century, it shows in its decoration the influence of Austrian and French 'Rococo, while from the mid-century it toQk the Antiquarian turn. Towards the end of the same century, occasional Greek revival manifestations appeared.

Ducth architecture took a substantially different course. Lieven de Key and Hendrik de Keyser (1565-1621 l developed the early Dutch style. usually plainer than the Belgian. It matured a Palladian phase of considerable dignity and quality in 1625 to 1670, where positive. austerity was practiced wherein external decoration being almost wholly excluded. Next, Daniel Mar.ot a Huguenot refugee, introduced the masculine style of Louis XIV to the Dutch court, effective in influencing interior decoration rather than architecture proper, and t ·:enceforward French fashions continued to be followed, though with sober external expression and bold and effective planning.

1. The Chancellery, Bruges (1535) a town house has.seemingly precocious Baroque qualities which are in fact due to the perpetuation of the flamboyant Gothic spirit. It has a two-storeyed facade with quasi-Doric orders, mullioned and transomed windows, and central gable with side-scrolls, crocl<ets and figures.

kids.content: 2. The Mussee' Plantin-Moretus, Antwerp (1550) is more authentically classical, and its extent and character illustrates the opulence and social status of a highly successful flemish burgher.

3. The Town Hall, Antwerp (1561 -6) is an imporant prototype of Belgian Early Renaissance. It has superimposed orders between closely-spaced large windows, a rustical basement storey and a galleried upper storey. Its centre-piece is highly characteristic of the phase, with its freely manipulated classical detail and generous use of plastic ornament.

GUILD.HOUSES, Grand' Place, Brussels erected by various guilds, Archers (1691) Shipmasters (1697), carpenters (16971,·printers 11697), Butchers (1720), Brewers (1752), tailors and painters, are·late Belgian-Baroque and Rococo fantasies which with their serried gable fronts and large window areas follow types established by the 16th century guild houses in Antwerp, and indicate the wealth of Flemish and Brabatine guilds of craftsmen and tradesmen.

1. The TOWN HALL, Leyden (1594} by Lieven de Key, owes something of its inspiration to Antwerp town hall, but is especially noteworthy as an example of the strapwork, fretwork and other petty ornament.

kids.content: 2. The Royal Palace, Amsterdam (1648-65) is a major example of Dutch civic architecture on an unusually large scale. Its style is palladian in the sense that it is of clear simple ordinance with no important departures from classical rule and that there is no intrusion of ornament on to the architectural lines. There is however, a greater freedom in the design of an open cupola-turret over the central, shallowly-projecting pavilion of the two-tiered pilastered facade, standing on a low basement storey and the crowning pediment has an infilling of petty sculpture.

kids.content: The 'age of revivals' is a common descriptive title for the years covered by this chapter in British architectural history, also known as of lnnoyation'. Paradoxically, it was one in which major new developments in the construction and planning of buildings were often combined with stylistic revivalism, varying in character from the antiquarian to the free interpretation of assumed historical principles. ·

Social and Technological influences arose·from the demands of a rapidly growing population within a society in the throes of the industrial revolution. Major inventions in metalurgy, cotton manufacture and the development of steam-power in the latter half of the eighteenth century ordained the course of the nineteenth. Increased birth rate contributed to the rise in population. Urbanization developed similarly the housing of the new urban population created acute social problems and thretened public health through overcrowding, inadequate sanitation and impure water supply.

The growing industrial areas were supported by new transport systems. A canal network was constructed from 1757 which eventually linked London to Kendal and the·Mersey to Humber. Railways prematurely terminated canals' profitability and the first rail Iinks between cities, the liverpool to Manchester line, opened in 1830. One Architectural, effect of canal · and railway facilities was that the cheapest building materials, common brick and Welsh State, became readily available anywhere and displaced local materials, causing a marked decline in local crafts and vernacular traditions of building from 1840 onwards.

The expansion of the towns meant that greater numbers of conventional buildings were required, such as house, theatres and churches. In adc;lition, entirely new types of buildings were necessary, such as the railway station, and many existing building types were transformed by new requirements.

list items.content: a. Town hall and to serve greatly expanded municipal business.
b. The hospital had to meet new medical practice requiring the p.::ovilion plan.

c. Commercial organizations evolved new methods as when those in banking produced the public bank, and those in the textile trade the warehouse while changes in the retail trade led to the evolution of the department store.

d. Innovations of type or function include a.l.most all classes of buildings, and country houses, swimming baths, fire and police stations, exhibition halls, university buildings, art galleries and many examp.les of buildings for transport and Industry.

kids.content: Although secular influences were predominant in determining the architectural requirements of the age, religious buildings are amongst its most significant works. The non conformist revival of the eighteenth century continued as one important factor of religious life, but the Catholic emancipation Act of 1829 in extending religious tolerance sanctioned church building of greater influence in work by A.W.N. Pugin (1812-52) the,. . theoist and designer.

As has already been indicated, advances in scientific knowledge and technology were fundamental to nineteenth- century progress steam - power generated many uses, providing motive power for tr(!nsport, and innumerable industrial purposes, thus leading to the enlargement of industrial buildings to take full advantage of the capacities expensive equipment. The invention of the process of making coal-gas about 1000 led to gaslighting in factories from 1807 and thereby made extended working hours more feasible.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile924.png

kids.content: Equally far-reaching innovations in buildings were often related to progress in general technology. Example in mettalurgy, and some were of great architectural importance one was the development of iron, dramatically illustrated by the construction of the Iron bridge at Coalbrookdale, Shropshire, in 1779. Cast-iron was soon adopted for architectural purposes.

The combination of cast-iron-and glass, a material also produced by new methods, led to the development of a novel building technique derived from construction of greenhouses, the most spectacular example being the crystal palace, erected in Hyde Park, London, for the great exhibition of 1851.

Wrought-iron, twice as expensive as cast iron was not used as much as the ·tatter for structural purpOses for this reason, but its tensile properties were exploited to provide ties, bolts and trusses and to meet special requirements. Steel was produced in quantity through the Bessemer process from 1855, but it was not used for general building until the 1880's when rolled sections were manufactures and replaced wrought-iron in the construction of wide spans.

The advent of reinforced concrete mass concrete incorporating steel bars, introduced a material capable·of withstanding great compressive and tensile loads, like steel. but with the further important advantage of a high degree of fire-resistance. Further the materials could be cast in any form, theoretically freeing architects from the traditional constraint of the rectilinear plan.

GAS lighting, refined and introduced into houses in 1840 were replaced by electricity in the 1890s. Central heating made larger windows possible, and the repeal of the burden some excise on glass in 1845 made them cheaper and resulted in an increased use of plate glass, produced by a new mechanical process. These influences on fenestration produced lighter interiors.

Great improvements in urban life also occured through advances in drainage and sanitation, with the introduction of the water closert, effective main drainage, and the provision of pure water, with the latter often piped from major catchment areas, of greater significance to the actual form of buildings was the invention of the Lift or elevator. Earliest liftsoperated on a· counter-weight system and were used for goods only, but in 1854 the American Elisha Craves Otis (1811-61) invented a rachet-and-pawl safety system.

Not only were nineteenth-century buildings shaped by new, complex reQuirements, social:, and technical, but they were commissionaI by new types of patron. The growth of a middle class of professional and business men created a type of patron no longer likely to be familiar with matters of taste and architectural values. Nor was the inexorable tide of change described. The custom of the eighteenth century had either placed the architect under direct patronage or had made him virtually synonymous with.the master-mason, in which capacity
· it was common practice for the architect to act as a contractor, an arrangement to
abuse and giving ample cause forthe lowreputation ofsuch practitioners. Byformingan ef-

fective professional association architects endeavoured to rectify this state of affairs. In 1834 the institute of British Architects was founded and classes of membership and a code of pro-fessional conduct were created; three years later a Royal charter of incorporation was granted. The establishment of close-professionalism with entrance by examination was a contentious process which advanced slowly: in 1882 admission to associateship became subject to examination.

Wealth, commerce and technical inventiveness characterize Victorian Britain and were cipal architectural influences, associated with her position as the leading industrial nation, until rivalled by Germany and America in the 1800s. The possession of an empire with vast natural resources, and the enjoyment of stable government at home and freedom from major wars, abroad, all contributed to the creation of the material prosperity of which Victorian

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile925.png

kids.content: The most conspicuous characteristic of Victorian and architecture is its diverse use of historic styles, inherited from the eighteenth century in the forms of Classical and Gothic.Revivals, in the inspiration drawn from 'picturesque' values, often reflected in multicolored, strongly textured buildings of highly informal design, and in the spirit of Eclecticism which informed its taste for exotic forms of architecture. Nineteenth century eclecticism combined native and foreign styles of almost all periods.

New functions and techniques produced new forms, but orthodox materials remained prevalent, stone and brick being used externally until towards the end of the century when probably as an answer to the severe atmospheric pollution. The use of Faience became common.

Because external walls were load-bearing, a conventional arrangement of windows was followed although these became larger and had fewer glazing-bars after 1845, the coming of the plate glass. The cast iron frame, another characteristic device of the period, was used internally and resulted in larger buildings, with more storeys than previously, to meet practical reQuirements and make the maximum use of urban sites. Customarily, urban commercial buildings were four or five storeys high until the introduction of steel-framing about 1905, and between then and 1914 eight or nine storeys became more generaL

In the nineteenth century, the classical tradition showed astonishing resilience. During the first decades the Greek revival flourished anc! was followed in the 1840s and 50s by a GraecoRoman phase of great magnificence, used for public buildings.

The palazzo was a triumph of national eclecticism; it.did not require symmetry of the classical orders, allowed unrestricted size, permitted a wide range of fenestration, perfectly accomodated a cast-iron frame system, and provided a powerfully expressive architectural form with flattering social connotations.

Parallel with but less general than the Italian mode, a revival of French Renaissance precedents from the mid-50s, the time of the Angl.o-french Alliance during the Crimecen war. Its most prominent characteristics were the Mansard roof and rather florid or-
and it was particularly popular for hotels and the more lavish town houses.

In 1880s Gothic revivalists endeavoured to develop the more rational procedure of emulating Gothic principles rather than inventing stylistic adaptations, however original. This produced one of the characteristic forms of the late Victorian phase, a freely interpreted version of Gothic. In churches the nave became the dominating feature by its great height, breadth and a clearly defined bay system. Decorative detail was much simplified and made subservient to mass, and was often Gothic in name only.

An important influence from the eighteenth century was the taste for the 'Picturesque' reflected in the predilection for highly textured, colorful materials, asymmetry and informality. These features appear in some degree in all phases of Victorian Gothic, and the penchant for asymmetry appears to have affected even Alexander 'Greek Thomson in his designs for Glasgow churches, three particular instances of picturesQue influences are:

kids.content: *Picturesque - term in a specialized sense to describe one of the attitudes of taste towards architecture and landscape gardening in the late 18th and early 19th century; buildings and landscape were to have the controlled informality of a picture.

Hybrid buildings combined masonry and iron-and-glass structural elements. The use of wrought-iron on a large scale for expressly architectural purposes appears to have been chiefly decorative than structural.

The new Architectural concepts of 1880s and 1890s combined with the possibilities produced by the introduction of steel and reinforced concrete led to the design of a heterogenous group of buildings of strikingly progressive character between 1900and 1914.

kids.content: The Clifton Suspension Bridge, Bristol (1830-63) designed by lsambard Brunei, aversatile and imaginative engineer was carried out contrary to the recommendation of Thomas Kelford. The principal span of 214m over the 76 m deep gorge is suspended on chains from a previous bridge by Brunei, the Hungerford Bridge, London. The pylons supporting these are Egyptian in character and Brunei intended that they should be faced with metal plates stamped with hieroglyphics. Antiquarianism and the idea of grandeur matching grand.eur are characteristic Early Victorian attitudes.

St. George's Hall Liverpool (1840-54) by Harvey Lonsdale Elmes, is the most magnificent Neo-classical monument in Britain. Elmes succeeded in winning two separate competitions for a concert hall and for assize courts for Liverpool in 1839 and 1840. The planning is strongly oxial, but satisfies the complex requirements ingeniously, and the different elements are freely expressed externally. The main portico has a double row of eight corinthian columns, and the east and west elevations are eseentially symmetrical.

WESTMINSTER NEW PALACE (Houses of Parliament}. London (1836-68} by sir Charles Barry is a non-classical design which was imposed by the competition conditions. Three important trends emerged from the design: the authentics Gothic detail, supplied by Pugin reflects the.antiquarian character of the contemporary Gothic revival; the formal but not fully symmetrical planning by Barry, which had to accomodate the surviving west minster hall from the fire of 1834, reveals the continuing potency of

kids.content: The CRYSTAL PALACE. London (1850-1) designed by Sir Joseph Paxton, was one of the most remarkable buildings in nineteenth-century in Britain. Although the Great Exhibition, for which it was built, is generally considered to belong to the high Victarian Epoch, the building of the Crystal Palace rests firmly on Early Victorian technology. It was erected originally in Hyde Park and was moved to Sydenham in 1852-4. Paxtons' idea was for a giant conservatory with a cast-iron frame and the ridge-and furrow glazing system he had developed for the chats with conservatory. In cross section the building somewhat resembled a double-aisled basilica, rising in thr.ee tiers, the lowest 124.4 m wide, the next (the inner aisles) 80.4 m and the nave topmost 36.5 m. However, the 'aisles' and 'nave' were divided from one another by tiered open galleries 73 m wide, so that the actual span of the 'nave' was only 22m. The transept had the same width as the nave but was barrel-vaulted. In this colossal project of pre-fabricated building, vast quantities of iron and glass and other materials, as well as scrupulous organization to allow the work to be completed in so short a time, Paxton had as engineer-associated Sir Charles Fox while Owen Jonee, was responsible for the decoration.

list items.content: B. HIGH VICTORIAN (1850-1870)

kids.content: ALL SAINTS. Mongaret Street, Westminster (1849-59) by William Butterfield, is a truning point in the Gothic revival and the first church to incorporate polychromy in its construction. It stands with a parsonage and choir school on an extremely cramped site, creating a striking effec by its unusual character and lofty spire. Typical features are the harsh, angular forms, the brick construction and the highly durable materials used to form permanent decoration in 'constructional polychromy'. Internally, geometrical patterns decorate the walls and fittings in multi-coloured marbles and tiles and alabaster.

*Polychromy - a term originally applied to the art of decorative painting in many colours, extended to the colouring of sculpture to enhance naturalism, also described to the application of variegated materials to achieve brilliant or striking effects.
Church, Choir School and Parsonage Interior: nave and chancel All Saints, Margaret Street, london

kids.content: The UNIVERSITY MUSEUM, Oxford (1855-9) designed by Benjamin Wood'{"ard (1815-61) is a landmark of high Victorian Gothic arch.itecture. The main front has a narrow, steeply-roofed central feature, containing the entranee door flanked by two-storey wings in which there are regularly-spaced windows of Italian Gothic style. In the steep roofs of the wings there are triangular dormers in two series, the upper extremely small. The walls are of cream-coloured bath stone, with inset marbles around the doorway head and upper-window arches, and the roofs are patterned in purple and grey-green slates. Internally, there is a quadrangle roofed with iron and glass; the ironwork is decoratively 'Gothicized' with elaborate ornament. The roof is upon clustered and banded iron pillars, from which spring arcade ribs, the latter reaching to the apex of the glazed, pitched roof. The covered quadrangle is itself walled about by polychrome arcades.

kids.content: RED HOUSE, BEXLEY HEATH, KENT (1859-60} built by Philip Webb for William Morris, so named because its materials, redbrick and tiles, represent a striking change from the normal pretentious and heavily stylized dwelling of the period. The design is rationally eclectic rather than stylistically pure Gothic; although the general effects of high-pitched roofs anq pointed arches is Gothic in character. Nevertheless, 'Sash windows' were used for practical reasons as were the pointed arches which span them. The planning is informal and unconventional. The different elements of plan and structure are expressed in accordance with Puginesque principles.
*Ecc/esiastism- the selection of elements from diverse styles for architectural decorative designs, particularly during the second half of the 19th century in Europe and U.S.A.
"'Sash window - a double-hung usually wooden, glazed frame or sash, designed to slide up and down in grooves with the aid of pulleys.

Voysey_created a distinctly individual style of house by means of massive hipped roofs, plain, white, rendered walls with sloping buttresses. Continuous ranges of mullioned windows, with those at first floor level placed immediately below the eaves. and wide doorways, often decorated with simple cut-out heart shapes.

kids.content: The French Revolution of 1789 and the Napoleonic Empire left indelible marks upon Europe. At its zenith, in 1810, the Empire comprised the whole of France, Belgium, the left bank of the Rhine, Holland and the German coast as far as the Western Baltic, as well as those states which retained individual governments under the authority of the i=rensh emperor; Switzerland, Spain, the Kingdom of Naples and the lllyrian provinces. Inevitably French influences was paramount and affected most aspects of life, a factor of especial consequence being the code of Napoleon which laid the foundations of modern continental law.

In 1830, almost the whole of the continent erupted in revolt-in France where the Bourbon monarchy {restored after the eclipse of Napoleon) tottered, but found bried uneasy survival under the more liberal Louis-Philippe; in Belgium which achieved national identity and independence.

In general terms it can be said that between 1830 and 1870 Europe was imbued by liberal and national movements, while after 1870 she was increasingly dominated by power politics, based largely on the economic rivalry of France and Germany, which led eventually to the first world war, in which Germany was allied with Austria and France with Belgium, Russia, Italy and later the U.S.A. France and Germany were administered by bureaucratic systems; the former retaining the liberal and democratic traditions she had pioneered; the latter, marked by a particularly harsh militarism.

Technological developments were reflected in the growth of communications, particularly railways. Belgium, Holland, France and later Germany acquired substantial colonies. In this way, aided by advances in ship design including the introduction of stel'lm-power, new and wide communication links were formed. Particutarty important as a link with the East was the'Suez Canal, the work of the Engineer Ferdinand de Lesseps (1805·94). Opened in 1869.
The enthusiasm of the age for technical progress and commercial endeavour was expressed tn the series of international exhibitions of science and industry held. In Paris in 1855, 1867,

.'878 and 1889 1900. In all cases the exhibition _buildin_g.s struction. It was for the same exhibition that the Engineer Gustave Eitfel (1832-1923) design/ /1/' ed the famous 300-metre (1985-foot) high Eiffel tower. J ·

kids.content: Throughout the century France made important contributions in structural design and also in the development of reinforced concrete construction.

In religious matters the period was generally ma{ked by tolerance. With the growing concern for national sovereignty and the increasing competition between the European·nations, authority in the catholic church became more and.more centred on Rome, and ultramontanism prevailed.

The achievements of the nineteenth century especially in science and technology. were great and the pride .and self confidence of the age understandable. Coupled with the ''heroic" view of man, inherited from romanticism, it seemed that all things were possible and that man-European man, that is-was indeed 'master o'f his fate'.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile943.png

kids.content: In spite of widening eclecticism, the Roman and Greek forms popular during the Napoleonic era continued to be used. The round arch, Florentine, Romanesque and Byzantine as well as Roman, was a popular motif especially in Germany, where the term RUNDBOGENSTIL was coined to describe buildings employing it. France was particularly influential, especially through the publications of E.L. Boullee's pupil, Jean-Nicolas- Louis Durand (1760-1834) who, ·after serving as an Engineer in Napoleon's army, had been appointed Professor of Architecture of the Ecole Polytechnique on its establishment in 1765 his system of design was based on the repitition of standard bays, both in plan and elevation, which could be enriched with classical, Mediaeval or Renaissance motifs as desired, it provided a convenient, though often dull, formula for the design of the large, complex buildings required by the age. In principle, it had an affinity with the bay system., pragmatically adopted With the introduction of iron construction.

As in Britain the period was marked by a revival of Italian forms, already used in the RUNDBOGENSTIL but seen in a much more developed way in the work of F.l.J. Duban {1797-1870), and in the exterior of Henri Lal:\rouste's library of S. Genevieve, Paris. The use of iron in building increased.

Covering the period of the French Second Empire, this phase is comparable with the high V.lctorian in Britain. During it, the Renaissance Revival became more firmly established and took on a new richness. Pavilions and high mansard roofs elaborate metal crestings added sky-line interest, while wall surfaces were relieved with often opulent decoration of a cinquecento character. ·

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile944.png

kids.content: The phase was marked by a number of major town planning undertakings, the most important being the replanning of Paris by Baron Eugene Georges Hauss-mann (1809-91) between 1853 and 1868. Of considerable importance are buildings associated with the growing interest in Gothic Architecture and the structural use of iron. To generalize, it be said that during this phase France maintained her leadership in both academic and innovatory architecture.

Euthusiasm for metallic construction intensified and was audaciously displayed in the Paris exhibitions of 1878, and especially 1889. While in the 1873 internationai.Exhibition at Vienna an iron Cupola, 107m 1350 ft.) in diameter, was built, the largest structure of this sort of the century. The Paris department store, had a floor area of over 2,500 square meters was almost entirely of iron and glass.

Academic architecture as represented by the Ecole des Beaux-Arts prevailed through most of the continent. There was a tendency to turn increasingly to Antique as opposed to Renaissance forms, as in the Victor Emanuel II monument,Rome(began 1885) but a Baroque scale and 'imperial richness were maintained, sometimes in an excessively ponderous way.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile945.png

kids.content: In Holland and Scandinavia, inspired by mediaeval examples and the ideas of Viollet - le - DUC, there was a movement towards a less pretentious, more humane and at the .same time rational, architecture. hi both cases, brick, which was the traditional material of the regions, was extensively used.

In Spain in the 1880s there was a sudden and extraordinary creative flowering in Barcelona in· the work of Antoni Gaudi (1856 to 1934). In its plasticity of form, his work might appear to be linked to, and indeed anticipate ART NOVEAU, but the latter has connections with the linear forms of metal construction and the malleable properties of wrought iron and steel. From the end of the century until the war, Europe was a ferment of new ideas in architecture.
An art free from any historical style and characterized by forms of for ornamentation in the facade aptly called for Floral style.

The termArt Noveau styte involved theHcr.ea!ion I) atmosphere in.which the freely shaped, writhing forms of the designers seem to gesticulate in their own way at the current historicism of the more conventional work of the time. It possessed no single stylistic purpose or intention as far as one can see, other than that given to at by each individual designers.

There were however, many common charactetistics. The Art Noveau designer showed a delight in the dynamic forms found in nature, as welt as in the -deliberate simpncation of structural elements buildings and building interiors.

It was a romantic phase that took pride in the handmade object. This aspect of the style was mainly "confined to Ornamentation" and to interior design and furniture production.. The naturalistic ornament was applied in a typically mannerist way accentuating the delicate but vigorous twists found in nature into exaggerated design effects.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile947.png

kids.content: Guimard was the chief expQnent of the Art Nouveau style in Paris. The entrance to the Castel Beranger fJJ indicates a much freer kind of decoration than his later wrought-iron Metro entrances, which are as famous as Lautrec's posters and characterize, to this day, the Belle Epoque. He developed a number of station types, including entrances with fan-shaped and enclosed pavilions (2} and others with balustrades.

The Elvira Studios at Munich, Demolished long ago, the facade has fascinated historians of Art Nouveau for many years. In reality little is known about its origins as a design, but as a symbol of the youthful exuberant German "new art" style it is unequalled. Designed in 1.896 by August Endell, whose work owes a debt to Japan, it has a book illustrater's panache yet embodies very largely the theoretical framework which Endell, who trained as an aesthetician as well as an architect, established for his turn-of-the-century architecture. He spoke in his writings about forms having certain qualities of "lightness", "sharpness" and "speed".

DOMESTIC BUILDINGS Court Gardener's House, Charlottenhof, Potsdam (1829-31) by Schinkel, is a remedelling of an existing building in a highly picturesque way, inspired by contemporary English· taste. Its low-pitched roofs, overhanging eaves and assymetrically placed. belvedere- like elements derive from Italian vernacular sources.

kids.content: Schloss Linderhof, (1870-86), by Georg von Dallmann, was built for Ludwig II of Bavaria in the South -German Rococo style. It is superbly sited with delightful formal gardens and sumptuous and finely rococo interiors.

ThePalauGuell.Barcelona(1885-9)also.by .. , Gandi, seems to presage Art Nouveau in its . forms. Among the building's many novelties, especially interesting are the twin parabolic portals with their grilles of curvilinear ronnwork, the cantilevered first floor, and the conscious asymmetry in the placing of elements.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile950.png

kids.content: The Casa Balto, Barcelona (1905-7) is an important example of Gandi's mature work. The stone dressings of the lower part of the facade are modelled plastically in sinuous and ovoid forms, echoed in the metal balustrades above, while around the rectangular upper windows, the wall surface is studded with fragments of coloured glass.

Casa Mila. Barcelona (1905-10) by Gandi represents a further development. Undulating stone facades enclose an irregular mesh of polygonal rooms, no two alike, and none with right-angled corners, externally swept into heavy browns over the tiers. Of roll-edged, round-angled windows with intricate iron balconies.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile951.png

kids.content: No. 6, Rue Paul-Emile Janson {Hotel Tassel), Brussels by Victor Horta, is generally regarded as the first complete building in fully-fledge Art Noveau style. It is a narrow-fronted and deep, the rooms planned rather more freely than was normal at this time and with some exploitation of floor levels. The main element of the generally unobstrusive facade is a segmental oriel bay with metal mullions and window heads and decorative iron balustrades. The interior, particularly in the staircase-hall and salon, provides striking examples of ART Noveau. Iron is widely used for both structure and decoration and is. developed into free-following linear plant-like forms, echoed in the mosaic floor decoration.
The Votivkirche, Vienna (1856-79) by Heinrich Von Ferstel, a rich and elaborate
·essay in Gothic with tall, slender western towers with open belfries and crocketted steeples, was the result of competition held in 1853·.

The Church of the SACRE' COEUR, Paris (1875-7) design of Paul Abadie, largely completed by the end of the century, but not wholly finished until 1919 stands with a cluster of white domes on the heights of Montmartre. It reflects Byzantine influence by way of the mediaeval cathedral of St. Front, Pedigueux.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile952.png

kids.content: The Church of the SAGRADA FAMILIA. BARCELONA, (1882-1926) by Antoni Gaudi, who took over the work in 1884, still largely unfinished, has the same fantastic qualities seen in other buildings by this architect. the 'south transept' facade comprises a trio of steeply gabled, deeply recessed porches, the two lesser on the flanks corresponding to the transept aisles dominated by four skittle 0 shaped openwork spires. The porches are profusely ornamented with sculptured naturalistic floral and figure ornament which although in stonework, has the effect of soft, melting snow. Enormous faceted finrals, studded with broken coloured tiles, cap the four towers. The inner arcades were to have been inclined towards one another and were intended to give the semblance of weird, angular trees, stark branches, reaching upwards tos sustain a stalactite vault, over the nave and flat roofs over the double aisles, again with stalactites, between which scores of circular 'eyes' would admit shafts of daylight. Art Noveau was never so plastic, dramatic or eccentric.

The Schauspielhaus, Berlin 0819-20) by K.F. Von Schinkel, a powerful work in the Greek revival style, is marked by the strong, geometric control of its elements, the building taking the form of a series of boldly articulated rectangular masses. The entablature of the pedimented hexastyle Ionic portico is continued around the building, binding together its main forms. A high, pedimented attic, expressing the central auditorium, dominates the building with, on each of its faces, opening grouped together as continuous bands, divided by rectangular, pilaster- like mullions. The building is a masterpiece of Neo-classicism.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile953.png

kids.content: The Altes Museum, Berlin (1824-8). by Schinkel, is Greek revival in style and an example of the application of Durand's planning principles to a new 19th century type. Four long two-storeyed gallery wings, each planned on a regular bay system, from the sides of a square, in which is inscribed a large, circular hall rising the full height of the building, with an ambulatory at first floor level communicating with the upper galleries, and surmounted by a patheon-like the latter expressed externally as a simple attic. The museum is entered through a deep Ionic colonnade of 18 columns, embracing the full two storeys of the building and extending across its entire width, COI\tained by flank walls treated as antae.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile954.png

kids.content: Thorwaldsen Museum, Copenhagen (183-48) by M.G.B. Bindesboll was built to house the work and collections of the Danish sculptor BertiI Thorwaldsen. Greek revival in style, the bold severity of its astylar forms recalls the work of Schinkel, and to some extent Egyptian architecture, especially in the internal courtyards. The barrel-vauited ceilings of the galleries are decorated in the Pompeiian style.

The LIBRARY of St. Genevieve, Paris (1845-50) by Henri Labrouste, was the first french library to be designed as an individual building and, externally; is a brilliant example of Neo-Renaiss&nce design. Internally, it has a complete iron frame the metal double roof being supported by three rows of iron building 80 M x 23M, with a rear projection containing a double staircase, the lofty main floor stands above a shallow ground floor, and is covered by 21ongitudinal barrel with iron arch-ribs springing from the central line of columns, with panels between of thin, reinforced plaster. A low-pitched, metal outer roof Sf)ans the full width of the building.

kids.content: The National LIBRARY (1862-8) by Labrouste, shows further advances in planning room is covered with a series of nine pendentived simple domes of terra-cotta, each pierced at its crown.with an 'eye' providing natural top light, supported by twelve slender columns of iron arranged in four rows, the outer columns standing close to the walls. The vaults, arch-soffits and the wall surfaces above bookstack level are enriched with delicate decoration. The stack room has-tiers of top lighted stacks with open gridded metal floors to allow light to pass to lower levels, flanking a central space, bridged at intervals by communicating gangways.

It consists of a vast platform with a terrace supporting an equestrian statue of the king, backed by an enormous, slightly·concave corinthian colonnade, supponing an elaborately decorated attic, and terminated at each end by poticoed pavilions, bearing great bronze sculptural groups. The building has a total height of 61 meters.

kids.content: The STOCK EXCHANGE (1898-1903} designed by H.P. Barlage, is of red brick with restrained stone dressings and,.despite strong Romanesque overtones, has a character of honesty an"d simplicity. Internally, the glass and metal roof is frankly exposed.

The OPERA HOUSE, Cologne 11870-2) by J. Raschdorf, a building of modest dimensions, affinities with French Neo-Baroque, recognizable in the steep Mansard roof, the "LUCAANE" or dormer windows ·and the disposition of the highly decorative, pavilion - like features on the otherwise asty!ar facades.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile958.png

kids.content: The POST SAVINGS BANK, VIENNA (1216 B), by OTTO WAGNER, retains, internally, in the semi-elliptical form of its metal and glassroof. a trace of the lightness associated with Art Noveau but other wise the building bears no readily identifiable historical associations.

D. COMMERCIAL BUILDINGS The HALLES CENTRALES. Paris, (1853) by Victor Baltard. were part of Haussrriann's plan for Paris and the main markets of the city. There are 12 pavilions. Planned as a series of board circulation routes, intersec- . ting at right angles·, with the areas between occupied by stalls, the complex was constructed of iron and glass and completely covered. Light was admitted mainly through clearstoreys between the eaves of the pitched roofs of the circulation routes and the lower roots over the stall areas.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile959.png

kids.content: GARE du NORD. Paris (1862-3) by Hittorff, a fine early railway station, has a superb iron and glass train shed and, externally, it shows a development of the Neo-classic character seen inthe architect's earlier work.

GARE de l'EST, Paris (1847-52) by F.A. OUOUESNEY, which has been greatly altered and enlarged; where the main front with two projecting Neo-Renaissance wings, linked by a one storey arcade, flanked by a great central semicircular window. eloquently expressing the idea of a communications 'gateways' and providing the focal point for Haussmann's Boulevard sebastopol..

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile960.png

kids.content: TURBINE Building. Menier chocolate works, Noiseii- Sur-Marne (1871-2) by Jales Saulnier, offers the earliest French example of a full skeleton-frame in iron. It stands upon massive stone piers over the river Marne, borne on double girders which carry an iron frame incorporating the floors and pitched roof. The stanchions and their bracing enclose, externally, brick panels of polychromatic patterning, the effect somewhat resembling half-timber work.

The ENTRANCE, PAVILION, International EXHIBITION, PARIS (1878) by GUSTAVE EIFFEL, made extensive use of . glass and iron. adapting these materials to currently fasionable architectural taste. Similar in the broad lines of its composition· to the later petit palais, the domes of the ce!')tral and end pavilions had large glazed luneities, one·on the central dome ·being projected downwards to form a deep, arched portaL Between·the three pavilions, the walls were punctuated by enriched metal stanchions and fully glazed.
*stanchion - a vertical steel support. Cast-iron was used until relatively cheap steel became available.

The GALERIE des Machines, International Exhibition, Paris, (1887) by the engineer Victor Contamin and the architect C.LF. Dutert was 427 M long. 45 M high and spanned 114 M. Its constituent steel principals formed four-centred arches, hinged at the apex and the base, where they tapered to their bearings. These principals were steel-braced. longitudinally and the hall was completely glazed.

kids.content: METRO STATION, Place de Ia Bastille. Paris (1900) by H. Guimard, a metal and glass construction, well illustrates the characteristic of Art Noveau. The linear expression of the metal, curved sinous of convoluted whereever structure allowed; the naturalistic, vegetal nature of the ornament; the lack of imposts on arches, as here on the dual horseshoe entrance; and the exclusion of historical references, are all typical of the style.

kids.content: Economically and Socially the most advanced nation of the continent was the U.S.A., where a sense of national identity had been reinforced by the war with Britain of 1812-14. By 1840 the country's trade was worth 250 million dollars per year, almost half being earned by New York. Cotton of Louisiana and extensive coal and iron resources of Pennsylvania developed rapidly.

The presidency of Andrew Jackson gave impetus to wider democratic ideals and greatly encouraged individual enterprise. The westward movement being accelerated by the discovery of gold in California in 1848.

The coming to power in 1861 of an anti-slavery government under Abraham Lincoln (1809-65) brought to a head the rivalry between the more dynamic Northern States and the cotton producing Southern States, with their long-established plantation system based on slavery, and kindled the tragic civil war {1861-65). during the course of which, in 1863, slavery was abolished. The victory of the Northern States, and of the union, was decisive for tl:le future of the country and encouraged industrial development, which in turn greatly increased-the rate of immigration generally, the period following-the civil war was one of continuing commercial expansion, an age offering great opportunities and high material rewards to individual industrialists, bankers, farmers and railway owners. This situation, clearly reflected in the architecture of the time,continued until the financial crash of 1929 and the ensuing depression. The opening up of the country by railways was essential to development, and the continent was finally traversed by rail from coast to coast in 1869. Alexander Graham Bell's invention of the telephone in 1876 further facilitated communications accross the vast country which. in 1865, had been linked to Europe by trans-Atlantic cable. Finally the mass production of the motor car between the two world wars further extended communications and movement.
As far as industry is concerned, Canada's development was much less rapid, her economy being based almost entirely on the export of lumber and wheat.

Like Canada. the .countries of South America relied on the export of natural products rather than on manufacturing, and the opening of the Panama Canal in 1914 was of great significance in the development of the countries of the Pacific Coast.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile965.png

kids.content: European influence in both North and South America remained strong throughout the period, although materials, local skills, social customs and especially climatic conditions played their part, and buildings continued to possess strong regional characteristics.

In the U.S.A. itself, a conscious striving for a truly 'national' architecture became evident soon after the war of independence, and architecture in that country can be considered as passing through three broad and loosely defined phases: ·

list items.content: a. Post-colonial (1790-1820) architecture of this period moved away from the English Georgian idiom which had become established along the eastern seaboard of the country Neo-classic elements·were introduced.

b. First Eclectic Phase (1820-1860) during this period the revived greek style was predominant receiving a more whole-hearted acceptance that it did in England and developing specifically American characteristics. The Gpthic and Egyptian styles found some popularity but compared with the Greek revival, these were minor streams.

kids.content: The type of timber- framing known as the 'baloon-frame' came into use during this period and revolutionized timber construction. As its name suggests, rather than relying on an essentially post-and-lintel construction, the baloon-frame owes its strength to the walls, roof, etc., acting as diaphragms. Compar.atively light timber sections are employed which are nailed together, floor and ceiling joists, forming ties, the whole stiffened by the external timber sheathing.
This period saw considerable developments in the use of cast-iron asabuilding material.

list items.content: c. Second Eclectic Phase {1860-1930) American architecture achieved inter.,·ational significance during this period and followed two main streams. The first related to the

kids.content: Gothic revival and initiated as a Romansesque revival with H. H. Richardson as itsfirstim-

portant exponent, gained considerable momentum and reached great vigour and vitality in the work of Louis Sullivan. In some respects the movement in its later stages can be equated with that of the arts and craft;> in Britain and it culminated in the work of Frank Lloyd Wright.

The second stream was more academic in character. Influenced by the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in P-aris its architecture inspired by the great periods of the past, the Italian and French Renaissance, ancient Greek and Roman and late Gothic.
Two important and influencial exhibitions belongs to this period; the centennial exposition 1876, Philadelphia and the world's Columbian exposition (Chicago 1893).

The period is noteworthy for structural experiment and achievement. The Skyscraper, often as America's greatest single contribution to architectural development, was a product of this phase and was closely related to metal frame construction the non-load-bearing :curtain waJI' and the left or elevator. The period saw also the establishment of many schools of architecture in the U.S.A., the first at Massachussetts institute of Technology in 1868, under W.R. Ware.

kids.content: 1. The WHITE HOUSE, Washington D.C. (1792-1829) the official residence of the president of the U.S.A. was designed by James Hoban, an Irish architect, in the English Palladian Style. After damage sustained in the war of 1812, it was restored and considerable restoration has been carried out in the present century. The porticoes were design.ed by B.H. latrobe.

kids.content: 3. ROBIE HOUSE, Chicago (1908} by Frank Lloyd Wright, is dominated externally by its strong horizontal lines which seem to make it almost one with the land on which it is built. Constructed of fine, small brick with low-pitched hipped roofs, the house is planned in an open and informal manner, interesting use being made of changes of level internally, the flowing internal spaces being generated by a central core containing stair· case and fireplaces.

kids.content: Monticello, near Charlottesville, Virginia (1793} was designed by Thomas·Jefferson third president of the U.S.A. For his own use. The first house, and elegant example of colonial Georgian, was completely remodelled in a free and imaginative Palladian manner.
BILTMORE, Ashville, North Carolina {1890-5) by A.M. Hunt, the first American architect to be trained at the Ecole des Beaux-Arts in Paris, in the style of an early French Renaissance chateau.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile971.png

kids.content: STOUGHTON HOUSE. Cambridge,.Mass (1882-3) by Mckim, Mead and White, is a timber-framed house, ita-walls-el8tfexternallywith wood providing an important example-of the so-called 'Shingle style'.

An external cladding of wood Shingles over a timber frame became popular In domestic building during the sectJnd half of the 19th century. Internally, the plan arrangement shows a loosening and foreshadows the 'Free .Plan', to be developed later by .Frank Uoyd Wright.

WINSLOW HOUSE, RIVER FOREST, Illinois (18931, the first important work of Frank Lloyd Wright, is a simple structure, basically symmetrical, but its'hipped roof, wide projecting eaves and emphatic horizontal lines foreshadow the architect's later work and what was to become known as the 'Praire House'.
TALIESIN EAST, Spring Green, Wisconsin (1911) by Frank Lloyd Wright.

The First CHURCH of CHRIST SCIENTIST. BERKELEY, CALIFORNIA (1910-121 by Bernard Maybeck, provided an antidote to the epedimic of old-Spanish-Mission revivalism. which was threatening to engulf architecture in California. It uses natural materials, and owes something to the vernacular tradition of the west coast of America.

kids.content: · (1872-7) by H.H. Richardson, is one of the key monuments of America architecture. The design: chosen competition, although basically Romanesque in character, is handled in a masterful and imaginative way. A Greek cross in plan, the building is dominated by a square central tower with round corner turrets, and is mainly of red granite, the rock-faced texture of which is exploited. Internal decoration in encaustic· colour was carried out by J.F. Lafarge, while the west porch was added in 1897 to the designs of Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge. GHUII.GHi806"n:>hl

UNITY TEMPLE, OAK PARK, ILLINOISS (1905-7) by Frank Lloyd Wright, is characterized by the sturdy simplicity of its external massing; on which the design relies rather than eclectic detail. In the building, the architect displayed a knowledge of and sympathy with the natural qualities of materials, which are here exploited both externally (in the pebble-faced concrete of the walls) and internally (in the sand-lime plaster work and natural timber details).

kids.content: C. EDUCATIONAL, CIVIC AND PUBLIC BUILDINGS

The STATE CAPrTOL, Richmond. Virginia (1789-98) by Thomas Jefferson, was based on a·Roman temple prototype, the Maisan Carree, Nimes. An ionic order was used by Jefferson, while for the Fenestration of the "cella" he had recourse to Palladian formulae. The building is regarded as the first truly Neo-classic monument in the U.S. and

kids.content: The UNITED STATES Capitol. Washington D.C. seat of the United States government, has become. with its crowning dome, one of the world's best-known buildings. The first building, erected to the designs of Dr. William Thorton, was planned on Palladian lines with a central rotunda; this has survived in essentials, despite numerous modifications and additions. After the war, B.H. Latrobe was responsible for rebuilding the structure. Between 1851 and 1867 additions were made by Thomas Ustick Walter who designed the flanking wings and great dome over the central rotunda, and was constructed largely of cast iron, with an internal diameter of 30m and a total height of 68 m.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile975.png

kids.content: The NATIONAL ACAQEMY of DESIGN, NEW YORK {1862-5} by P.B. Wight, Venetian (Gothic in style and making full use of polychrome masonry patterning, shows the influence of the writings of John Ruskin.

The PUBLIC UBRARY, BOSTON, Massachusetts (1887-93) by Mckim, Mead and White is beautifully detailed buildings, representative of the best in the academic stream of late 19th and early 20th century architecture in America. {Similar in elevation to the library of St. Genevieve, Paris).

The LINCOLN MEMORIAL WASHINGTON, D.C. (1911-22) by Henry Bacon, is in the form of an unpedimented Greek Doric peripteral temple,·set on a high podium and surmounted by a simple attic. Executed in white marble. its detail is superlatively refined and in its scholarship and execution marks a peak in academic architecture.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile976.png

kids.content: The CHAPEL and Post Headquarters, U.S. Military A·cademy, West Point, N.Y. romantically sited on a steep encarpment overlooking the Hudson River, are the work of Cram, Goodhue and Ferguson. and provide examples of academic architecture in Gothic style.
The Temple of Scottish Rite. Washington

D.C. (1916) a masonic temple designed by John Russel Pope, is in the same tradition as the Lincoln memorial. Externally, it takes the form of a reconstruction of the Mausoleum Halicarnassos, but is somewhat ponderously handled.

MERCHANTS EXCHANGE Philadelphia (1832-4) by William Strickland, is in the Greek revival style and is noteworthy for the grand, apsidal treatment of its rear elevation, enriched externally by a screen of Corinthian colum(ls rising from first-floor level through two storeys, and crowned by a cupola based on the Choragic monument of Lysi<:;rates, Athens.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile977.png

kids.content: The Marshall Field Wholesale Warehouse, Chicago, Illinois {1885-7) by H.H. Richardson, had seven storeys and was of load bearing wall construction. A remarkably powerful design, with its great arched openings and the vigorous texture of its masonry. it had considerable influence on later buildings in Chicago and elsewhere.

The Auditorium Building, Chicago, Illinois (1886-9) by Dankmar Adler and Louis Sullivan. combined with an opera house with hotel and office accomodation and owes much of its external character to Richardson's Marshall Field warehouse. Ten storeys high, it is of loadbearing wall construction built on spread foundations. Settlements has occurred to one side of the structure, in the tower which rises nearly 30m higher than the main building. Internally, the details are of high order. many showing a Byzantine character and some probably designed by Frank Uoyd Wright, who entered Sullivans's office as a draughtsman in 1887.

The MONADNOCK Building, Chicago Illinois (1889-911, by Daniel Burnham, has six teen storeys.. The building derives distinctior fro.m the simplicity of its elevational treatmen· and was the last tall building in Chicago fo which load-bearing walls were employed.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile978.png

kids.content: The SECOND Leiter Building. Chicago II· linois (1889·90l by W. Le B. Jenny, is an eight- storey metal framed building with a sim· pie and effective elevational treatment, the stone facade reading as a sheath over the internal metal structure.

The RELIANCE Building, Chicago Illinois (1890) by Burnham and Root, was originally built as a four-storeyed structure but was later extended to sixteen floors. The terra-cotta facing to the metal frame was reduced to a minimum and its simple yet carefully - detailed elevation the building marks an important advance in skyscraper design.

The GACE BUILDING, Chicago. Illinois (1898-9) by l ouis Sullivan and Holabird and Roche, is a three-Bay eight-storey framed structure, and fore shadows the elevational treatment of the Schlesinger-Mayer store.

kids.source: George Salvan Architectural Character and the History of Architecture_images/imageFile979.png

kids.content: The SCHLESINGER-MAYER STORE (189919041 by Louis Sullivan, was originally a ninestorey structure, a twelve-storey section being added in 1903-4 and further additions by D. H. Burnham. The building was originally crowned by a rich overhanging cornice. The white terracotta facing to the building's steel frame truthfully follows its structure, and horizontal lines a·re emphasized. The ground and first floors have cast-metal friezes richly decorated in low relief, providing first-rate examples of Sullivan's decorative work, in some ways sug· gestive of European Art Noveau. ·

The WAINWRIGHT BUILDING, St. Louis, MO. {1890-1) by Adler and Sullivan, a tenstorey steel-framed building, provided an answer to the elevation problem of the skyscraper. Vertical members of the frame are emphasized externally as brick piers, and the building is capped by a deep, richly decorated frieze, pierced by circular windows lighting the top floor, while the recessed panels between floors are similarly decorated.

The LARKIN SOAP CO. BUILDING Buffalo N.Y. (1904-51 by Frank lloyd Wright, was designed around a central circulation court, lit from the roof and sides by windows sealed from noise and dirt. Offices were approached from galleries around the court, borne on brick piers. Externally, the building was characterized by the simplicity and scale of its massing, which relied entirety on the relation of clearly articulated rectnagular forms. ·

kids.content: (1911-13) by Cass Gilbert, 241m high with fiftytwo storeys, was carried out in the Gothic style and provides an important landmark in the story of high building.

Soon after the completion of the Woolworth Building, the New York City zoning Ordinance (1916) became law. This had a profound effect on the form of New York Skyscrapers which, for reasons of light and ventilation, were ·now required to have certain minimum set-backs, related to their height. The effects of the ordinance can be seen in the Panhellenic House 1928 by J.M. Howells with twenty seven storeys and in the EMPIRE STATE BUILDING {1930-2) by Shreve, Lamb and Harmon, which rises through eighty-five storeys.

kids.content: Inspired by farmhouse architecture of Italian country villas. Most frequently identified by heavy wooden brackets under eaves, over doors and windows. Wings, towers, and bay windows commonly used. Windows tall and slender, often two-over-two. Rounded, poired windows appeared.

Composed ·of straight lines and right angles. A product of scrollwork and jigsaw. Narrow boards used on outside for reinforcement. Porch had diclgonal braces. Roof extended over front; gable ends formed separate plane.

More horizontal than vertical. Corner towers have witches' caps, appliqued sunbursts. Balconies with turned balustrades. Ivy-covered front porches. Roof lines an arrangement of varying shapes. A grand hall usually at interior core; other rooms radiate from it . Named after England's Queen ·Anne.

Sharply peaked roof line recalls thatch ed roots of English countryside. Houses have little roof overhang. Large expanses of wall space with few.

Picturesque compOSition . Built in Arnenca since 1880s. Half timbenng and massive medieval chimney. Identified by prominent gables and large,. expansive windows with small panes. Root often slate or tile. Also called Ehzabeth or Jacobean.

kids.content: A more refined style than ornate Queen Anne. Popularity due to America's preoccupation with revival styles. Many Roman and Greek elements: symmetrical faces; sensitive proportions, little ornamentation. Popu.larity ended with 1893 Columbian Exposition in Chicago.

City version of ornate Queen Anne. Resulted from fashionable trends and small city lots. Elaboration confined in orderly arrangements. Flush panels, flattened ornamentation, and few protruding parts. Even bay windows flattened. Facades decorated with swag garlands and plaster ribbons. Eaves enclosed.
Gambrel roof distinctive, recognizable characteristic. Wood shingles often us· ed for roof and siding. Cameo win· dows. Embodies cozy, informal intimacy.

Extremely popular during 1880s and 1890s. Direct descendent of the Victorian Queen Ann. Retains asymmetry, complex roof line. and large chimneys of Queen Anne style, but simpler. more restrained. Exhibits little exterior ornamentation. Lacks pretension, flamboyance. Large porches, double· hung windows. Cheaper to build than the Queen Anne.

kids.content: One-story with low overhanging roof and broad front porch. Unpretentious style, often rambling. Spreadout floor plan results in expensive-to-build house. Sometimes characterized as least house for most money. Convenience of everything on one floor accounts for widespread popularity. Modern ranch style house drect descendant of earlier, unpreter'ltious bungalow.

Modest second story distinguisKes semi-bungalow style. Also characteristic is broad, sloping roof with knee braces on eaves. Natural construction materials: fieldstone, shingles, stucco. Broad porches sometimes include attached arbors and climbing vines.
Simple, honest, practical. Few ornaments or frills. Built economical-
Extremely popular from turn of 20th century to 1920s. Characterized by boxlike shape and hip roof with dormer. A porch usually extends across front of house.
